cards.meaning: An encouraging remark praising someone’s positive attitude or determination.
cards.nuance: It sounds friendly and approving, but it can feel formulaic if you say it to someone who is struggling. Offer genuine encouragement when the person has shown courage or effort.
cards.literal: You have the right spirit or attitude.

uses.sentence: You handled the client complaint calmly; that’s the spirit we need this week.
uses.tip: Use it to reinforce a constructive attitude without sounding patronising.

uses.sentence: I nearly skipped the quiz, but I remembered your pep talk: that’s the spirit!
uses.tip: It works best among people who already share a light, playful tone.

uses.sentence: You stayed positive through several difficult calls; that’s the spirit we value in the team.
uses.tip: Pair it with a specific example so the praise feels meaningful.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older expressions linking “spirit” with a person’s attitude or character. The phrase became common as a spoken way of showing encouragement.

timeline.text: Older expressions used “spirit” to refer to someone’s temperament, energy or determination.
Forms resembling “that’s the spirit” appear in encouraging or approving contexts.
The shortened phrase remains a casual expression of praise and encouragement.

cards.pitfall: Avoid using it when someone has only made a small effort; specific praise usually feels more sincere.

cards.meaning: A way of saying you are sorry or disappointed about something unfortunate.
cards.nuance: It can sound sympathetic and casual, but it may also feel dismissive when the other person is serious about the problem.

uses.sentence: Your presentation was cancelled? That’s too bad, but I’m sure they’ll give you another slot.
uses.tip: Add a specific kind of support when someone is genuinely upset.

uses.where: Hearing bad news from a friend
uses.sentence: Your flight was cancelled? That’s too bad—I hope they can reroute you soon.
uses.tip: Follow it with a question or offer of help to show real concern.

uses.sentence: I’m sorry to hear the event was postponed; that’s too bad, especially after all your planning.
uses.tip: In sensitive writing, name the disappointment and offer practical help instead.

origin.summary: Likely developed from the plain meanings of “too” and “bad” before becoming a familiar conversational response to unfortunate news.

timeline.text: The words “too” and “bad” were used together to describe something seriously or excessively unfortunate.
“That’s too bad” became established in everyday English as a response to disappointing news.
It remains common in casual speech, though context can make it sound sincere or dismissive.

cards.pitfall: In a serious or emotional situation, “that’s too bad” can sound blunt; acknowledge the person’s feelings and show concern.

cards.term: the boot is on the other foot
cards.meaning: The situation has changed so that the roles or circumstances are now the reverse of what they were before.
cards.nuance: It highlights a reversal of control, responsibility or fortune. It often introduces a surprising twist or points out that someone is now in another person’s position.
cards.literal: A boot that was on one foot has moved to the other, turning the original image around.

uses.sentence: We spent the meeting persuading the client to help us, but now the boot is on the other foot.
uses.highlight: the boot is on the other foot
uses.tip: Use it to mark a clear reversal without becoming confrontational.

uses.sentence: He complained all evening about doing the dishes, but now the boot is on the other foot.
uses.highlight: the boot is on the other foot
uses.tip: It adds dry humor when someone experiences the frustration they described.

uses.sentence: We asked the vendor for an extension, so now the boot is on the other foot and they are waiting for our decision.
uses.highlight: the boot is on the other foot
uses.tip: Use it when the change in roles is important and you want the sentence to feel memorable.

origin.summary: Probably grew from older expressions about changing a boot or shoe from one foot to the other. The wording became especially familiar in British English during the 20th century.

timeline.text: Older expressions used changing a shoe or boot between feet as a picture of reversal.
The idiom took roughly its modern form in British English.
It remains a common way to describe a reversal of roles, responsibility or circumstances.

similar: the shoe is on the other foot
cards.pitfall: The phrase describes a reversal; it does not mean the situation has improved or worsened.

cards.term: the cat is out of the bag
cards.hint: a secret can no longer be kept
cards.meaning: A secret has been revealed, often before people were ready to share it.
cards.nuance: It sounds mildly informal and slightly dramatic. It works for news, gossip or a hidden plan that has become obvious.
cards.literal: A cat has escaped from a closed bag, making it impossible for the cat to remain hidden.

uses.sentence: The cat is out of the bag: the client will hear about the delay from another team.
uses.highlight: The cat is out of the bag
uses.tip: Use it when everyone already knows, then move straight to discussing what happens next.

uses.sentence: I was going to keep the party secret, but the cat is out of the bag.
uses.highlight: the cat is out of the bag
uses.tip: It adds playful drama when announcing news that was meant to stay secret.

uses.sentence: I won’t name names, but the cat is out of the bag and people are already asking questions.
uses.highlight: the cat is out of the bag
uses.tip: It softens the message slightly, but you still need to explain the situation clearly.

origin.summary: The modern phrase developed from older expressions about letting a cat out of a bag. Its exact figurative origin is uncertain, so stories about particular people are best treated as speculation.

timeline.text: Older wording included “let the cat out of the bag,” meaning to reveal a secret.
Similar expressions about the cat and bag began appearing in English writing.
“The cat is out of the bag” became the common form for an already revealed secret.

cards.opposite: the secret is still under wraps
cards.pitfall: Use it when information has genuinely been revealed; it can sound overdone for a minor update.

cards.term: the cure is worse than the disease
cards.hint: the remedy causes more harm than the problem
cards.meaning: The solution to a difficult situation creates more trouble or harm than the original problem.
cards.nuance: It often expresses frustration with a proposed fix, especially one that seems heavy-handed or costly. It can describe a real trade-off or exaggerate someone’s complaint.
cards.literal: A treatment makes the patient sicker than they were before treatment.

uses.sentence: Adding three approval steps may be the cure is worse than the disease.
uses.highlight: the cure is worse than the disease
uses.tip: Use it to question a proposed fix, then suggest a simpler alternative.

uses.where: Planning a celebration · dealing with rain
uses.sentence: Moving the whole party indoors is looking like the cure is worse than the disease.
uses.highlight: the cure is worse than the disease
uses.tip: It works well for humor, so deliver it with a light tone.

uses.sentence: Rebuilding the entire system would be the cure is worse than the disease, so let’s fix the immediate issue first.
uses.highlight: the cure is worse than the disease
uses.tip: Pair it with a concrete, less disruptive option.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the old idea that medical treatment can harm the patient as much as the illness. Its modern figurative use is older than its exact current wording.

timeline.text: The proverb appears in variations suggesting that the remedy may be worse than the sickness.
Similar forms become established in English writing about medicine and adverse remedies.
It is used broadly for clumsy, excessive or counterproductive solutions.

similar: a cure that causes more problems
cards.pitfall: The phrase is often a complaint rather than a full argument. Explain why the proposed solution causes the added trouble.

cards.hint: a mistake or harm that cannot be easily undone
cards.meaning: A harmful mistake or situation has happened, and the negative effects cannot easily be reversed.
cards.nuance: It says the main problem is already established, even if some consequences may still be managed or repaired. It often carries disappointment or resignation.
cards.literal: The harm has already been caused and cannot simply be undone.

uses.where: After a message sent to the wrong client
uses.sentence: The damage is done, so let’s focus on clarifying the situation and limiting the impact.
uses.tip: Use it to accept responsibility before shifting attention toward the next step.

uses.where: After accidentally sharing an embarrassing photo
uses.sentence: I tried to take the photo down, but the damage is done and everyone has already seen it.
uses.tip: It can express regret while acknowledging that the immediate problem has passed.

uses.where: Replying to a delayed delivery complaint
uses.sentence: The damage is done, but we can replace the order and provide a credit for the inconvenience.
uses.tip: Pair it with a concrete remedy so the message does not sound hopeless.

origin.summary: The wording comes from the older expression “the damage is done,” meaning that harm has already been caused. Its modern figurative use is well established.

timeline.text: The expression referred literally to harm that had already been inflicted.
The phrase began appearing in writing in contexts involving irreparable or already-completed harm.
It is used for mistakes, accidents and other situations whose main consequences cannot be undone.

cards.opposite: there's still time to fix it
cards.pitfall: It can sound final, so pair it with a practical next step if you need to reassure someone.

cards.meaning: A disagreement or argument becomes heated and sometimes chaotic.
cards.nuance: It suggests lively conflict involving strong feelings, raised voices or a sudden eruption. It is usually informal but can describe serious workplace disputes.
cards.literal: Birds fighting so vigorously that their loose feathers scatter through the air.

uses.sentence: The feathers fly when the team learns that another department has changed the deadline without telling us.
uses.tip: Use it when describing the atmosphere, not to blame a specific person.

uses.sentence: The feathers fly once everyone realizes that the birthday party was booked for the wrong day.
uses.tip: It adds a humorous touch when the argument is more dramatic than the issue.

uses.sentence: The feathers fly during the meeting after the customer discovers that nobody reviewed the revised quote.
uses.tip: Use it in informal reports; choose a more neutral phrase for formal documentation.

origin.summary: The idiom comes from the image of birds fighting so vigorously that feathers scatter around them. Writers later applied that image to heated arguments and conflict.

timeline.text: The literal image shows birds in violent or vigorous movement sending feathers into the air.
The phrase begins appearing in writing as a metaphor for quarrels and heated arguments.
It remains a vivid informal way to describe an argument or dispute.

cards.pitfall: The phrase does not necessarily mean people are physically fighting; it usually describes a noisy or heated argument.

cards.hint: too late to continue or win
cards.meaning: A situation, plan or contest has reached the point of failure, so continuing is pointless.
cards.nuance: It has a strong, theatrical tone and can signal final defeat, hopelessness or the end of someone’s plans. In friendly situations, it may be used playfully.
cards.literal: The contest has ended and its outcome has been decided.

uses.sentence: The game is up—we have no way to meet the deadline without another team helping us.
uses.tip: Use it to announce final defeat, but follow with what happens next.

uses.sentence: I caught you stealing the last card, so the game is up and you have officially lost.
uses.tip: It works as playful trash talk among people who know each other.

uses.sentence: Although we hoped to revise the proposal, the game is up: the client has chosen another supplier.
uses.tip: The dramatic wording suits a firm update, but can sound melodramatic in a routine email.

origin.summary: The phrase was recorded in English by the early 1600s. It originally described a contest whose outcome had been decided, then became a dramatic way of saying that a plan or struggle could not continue.

timeline.text: Literal sense: a contest has ended and the result has been settled.
English writers used the phrase to describe a failed contest or an enterprise that could not continue.
Shakespeare and other dramatists helped establish its theatrical sense of final defeat.
The phrase remains mainly dramatic, literary or playfully sarcastic.

cards.opposite: there is still a way to turn things around
cards.pitfall: It can sound overly dramatic for a minor setback, so save it for a genuinely final failure or a clearly playful exchange.

cards.term: the handwriting is on the wall
cards.hint: a warning that something is inevitable
cards.register: Common at work and in serious conversation
cards.meaning: The signs make it clear that a bad outcome or difficult change is likely to happen.
cards.nuance: This sounds grave and certain. Use it when evidence already points to a problem, not merely when you fear that one might occur.
cards.literal: Writing visible on a wall, like a warning or message for others to read.

uses.sentence: With three missed deadlines and no progress this month, the handwriting is on the wall.
uses.highlight: the handwriting is on the wall
uses.tip: Follow it with the specific problem and what needs to change.

uses.sentence: The empty dining room every Friday tells us the handwriting is on the wall.
uses.highlight: the handwriting is on the wall
uses.tip: It works best when obvious signs support your conclusion.

uses.sentence: The handwriting is on the wall: if testing slips again, we will miss the launch window.
uses.highlight: The handwriting is on the wall
uses.tip: Add concrete evidence so the warning does not feel exaggerated.

origin.summary: Likely developed from the older expression “the writing is on the wall,” which itself evokes a visible warning. The exact origin of the figurative meaning is uncertain.

timeline.text: The literal image is writing displayed where others can see and read it.
Similar expressions began to describe clear signs of an unwelcome future.
“The handwriting is on the wall” became a common idiom for an unavoidable warning.

similar: the writing is on the wall
the writing is on the wall
cards.pitfall: It is too strong for a vague worry; use it only when signs show that the outcome is already highly likely.

cards.hint: someone has been tricked or embarrassed
cards.meaning: Someone has been tricked, embarrassed or made a fool of, often because their plan backfired.
cards.nuance: This can be playful or pointed, depending on the tone. It often implies that the person thought they were one step ahead but ended up looking foolish.
cards.literal: The person is the target or butt of the joke.

uses.sentence: We planned to surprise the director, but the joke is on us because she already knew about it.
uses.tip: Use it lightly when acknowledging that a plan failed to work.

uses.sentence: I tried to sneak up on Sam, but the joke is on me because he was hiding behind the door.
uses.tip: It works well with friends when the mishap is harmless and everyone is laughing.

uses.where: Playful email · joking about a mistake
uses.sentence: I praised the new system before noticing it was offline, so the joke is on me.
uses.tip: Keep the tone friendly, especially if the message may be seen by colleagues.

origin.summary: The phrase probably grew from older theatrical and comic uses of “the joke” to mean the part of a performance that made people laugh. It later extended to people being tricked or made to look foolish.

timeline.text: The phrase referred to the joke or comic feature that amused an audience.
Its meaning expanded to include someone being mocked or embarrassed.
It is common informal speech for describing a harmless reversal or a successful piece of teasing.

cards.pitfall: This usually suggests the person has been made to look foolish; avoid it when describing serious humiliation.

cards.term: the lunatics have taken over the asylum
cards.hint: those in charge seem to be behaving irrationally
cards.meaning: The people in charge are acting irrationally, creating a chaotic or foolish situation.
cards.nuance: This has a playful, old-fashioned edge, but it can also sound harsh toward people you disagree with. It works best when the criticism is light and the people involved are absent.
cards.literal: The people believed to be insane have gained control of the institution meant to care for them.

uses.sentence: With three priority changes in one afternoon, I’m starting to think the lunatics have taken over the asylum.
uses.highlight: the lunatics have taken over the asylum
uses.tip: Keep it light; it can sound insulting if aimed directly at colleagues.

uses.sentence: Uncle Paul changed the route twice and ordered pizza for eight, so the lunatics have taken over the asylum.
uses.highlight: the lunatics have taken over the asylum
uses.tip: Use it about a situation, not as a serious diagnosis of anyone.

uses.sentence: The café opened for two hours, the menu is blank, and nobody knows where the owner is—the lunatics have taken over the asylum.
uses.highlight: the lunatics have taken over the asylum
uses.tip: It suits informal commentary rather than most professional writing.

origin.summary: The phrase probably grew from older expressions about madhouses and the people supposedly confined there. Its modern sense was established by the early 20th century.

timeline.text: Older sayings compared governing institutions, including the state and the Church, to a madhouse.
The wording “the lunatics have taken over the asylum” appeared in print as a humorous proverb.
It remains a theatrical, slightly old-fashioned way to describe disorder or irrational control.

cards.pitfall: The phrase labels people or their behavior as irrational, so avoid using it about coworkers or relatives in a serious argument.

cards.hint: something is hard to take in
cards.meaning: Someone finds a situation so strange, surprising or complicated that it is difficult to understand or imagine.
cards.nuance: It expresses shock mixed with disbelief or wonder. It often sounds conversational and dramatic, so it may be too informal for a serious official document.
cards.literal: The mind seems to become overwhelmed by an idea too strange or complex to process.

uses.sentence: When I saw the final figures, the mind boggles at how quickly they changed.
uses.tip: Use it with colleagues when you want to register surprise without becoming overly formal.

uses.sentence: He learned three languages in a year; honestly, the mind boggles.
uses.tip: This natural construction sounds more emphatic than saying a story is surprising.

uses.where: Travel blog · describing an astonishing place
uses.sentence: The underground cave stretched farther than I could see, and the mind boggles at what lies beyond.
uses.tip: It adds a personal note of amazement, so choose it for informal or semi-formal writing.

origin.summary: The expression likely developed from the idea of a person’s mind being confused, overwhelmed or unable to process what it encounters.

timeline.text: Related expressions used bog or boggle to describe a mind or person becoming confused or overcome.
The phrase appeared in British writing as a way of describing mental confusion or surprise.
It remains a familiar expression of astonishment and disbelief.

cards.pitfall: Use “the mind boggles” to express amazement; it does not mean that the situation is merely difficult.

cards.term: the oldest trick in the book
cards.register: Common at work and in conversation
cards.meaning: A well-known method that people have used many times before.
cards.nuance: It often sounds dismissive, suggesting that the tactic is predictable or outdated. Use it with light humor rather than when you want to avoid creating tension.

uses.sentence: Offering a discount without explaining the added value is the oldest trick in the book.
uses.highlight: the oldest trick in the book
uses.tip: It can make the criticism sound blunt, so soften it with a specific example.

uses.sentence: Saying you’re tired and leaving early is the oldest trick in the book, Alex.
uses.highlight: the oldest trick in the book
uses.tip: This is playful among friends but may sound accusing with someone you know less well.

uses.sentence: Adding more features without checking whether customers need them is the oldest trick in the book.
uses.highlight: the oldest trick in the book
uses.tip: Pair the phrase with evidence if the comment may affect a decision.

origin.summary: Likely grew from the idea that a book of tricks contains methods that are already familiar; the wording became a way to call something predictable.

timeline.text: The expression referred to a familiar trick found in an old collection of methods.
It was used figuratively for predictable tactics and arguments.
It remains a common dismissive phrase in speech and informal writing.

cards.pitfall: This phrase can sound insulting or cynical; consider naming the specific tactic instead of dismissing the person proposing it.

cards.hint: the fun or good time has ended
cards.register: Common at work and in everyday conversation
cards.meaning: The enjoyable or successful part of a situation has ended, and things are now difficult or disappointing.
cards.nuance: It can sound blunt, dramatic or disappointed, so use it when the change is clear and the people involved already understand the situation.
cards.literal: A party has ended, so the celebration and entertainment are finished.

uses.sentence: The project missed its deadline twice, and now the party is over.
uses.tip: Use it to signal that fun has turned into serious consequences.

uses.where: After a friend announces bad news
uses.sentence: When she heard the restaurant had closed, she said, “Well, the party is over.”
uses.tip: It can add dry humor, but it may sound harsh if someone is upset.

uses.sentence: Unfortunately, the party is over, so we’re postponing the launch celebration until next month.
uses.tip: It works when the bad news is definite and you want a slightly informal tone.

origin.summary: The phrase began by referring literally to the end of a social gathering, then developed a broader meaning for the end of a happy, successful or enjoyable period.

timeline.text: Literal sense: the social gathering has ended.
The expression appears in writing for the end of an enjoyable or successful period.
It is common informal English for announcing that good times have ended.

cards.opposite: the party is just getting started
cards.pitfall: This can sound too dramatic for a small setback; state the actual problem if you need a calm, neutral response.

cards.meaning: Someone suddenly understands what was happening or what someone meant.
cards.nuance: It often follows confusion, a poor explanation or a surprising piece of information. The phrase suggests that understanding arrived suddenly, rather than gradually.
cards.literal: A penny falls and hits the ground, making a small but noticeable sound.

uses.sentence: When Priya explained the deadline, the penny dropped for me: we had missed the earlier approval step.
uses.tip: Use it when a new explanation finally makes the situation clear.

uses.sentence: “You’re bringing your sister too?” Then the penny drops: she meant the whole group.
uses.tip: It suits informal speech and often adds light humour.

uses.sentence: Now the penny drops—you were asking me to review the file, not rewrite it.
uses.tip: Keep it conversational; it can sound abrupt in formal correspondence.

origin.summary: The phrase probably comes from the sound of a dropped penny, a familiar image in nineteenth-century Britain. Its figurative use for a moment of sudden understanding became established in the twentieth century.

timeline.text: The literal image of a penny falling and hitting the ground appears in British writing and speech.
The phrase develops the sense of a person suddenly understanding something.
It remains a common informal expression for a sudden realisation.

cards.pitfall: It means the moment of understanding has arrived; it does not mean someone has finally paid a small amount of money.

cards.meaning: A situation becomes more complicated, confusing or difficult.
cards.nuance: It often adds suspense or mild amusement, as though a story is revealing another unexpected twist. It can describe real events, especially when a problem starts becoming harder to handle.
cards.literal: In a story, the hidden plan or conflict becomes more intricate and harder to follow.

uses.sentence: The plot thickens when two teams realize they are working from different launch dates.
uses.tip: Use it when a problem is becoming more tangled than expected.

uses.sentence: Well, the plot thickens: half the guests have changed their plans, so we need a bigger table.
uses.tip: It adds a playful note when an already complicated plan takes another turn.

uses.sentence: The plot thickens after it emerges that the file was changed by two different people.
uses.tip: It works in informal reporting, but use plain facts in formal documents.

origin.summary: Probably grew from the language of theatre and storytelling, where a plot becomes more tangled as a story develops. Its figurative use became established as a way to describe complications.

timeline.text: The literal idea comes from a dramatic plot becoming more intricate.
The phrase appears in English writing about stories and theatrical plots.
It becomes common as a description of increasingly complicated real-life situations.

cards.pitfall: It usually suggests complications rather than a straightforward serious problem, so choose a more direct expression when you need to communicate urgency or risk.

cards.meaning: Everything remaining is easy, straightforward or unimportant.
cards.nuance: It is an informal, mainly British expression that suggests a task is already mostly done and only minor work is left.
cards.literal: After the main meal has been served, gravy can be poured over it; the remaining food is considered the easy extra.

uses.where: Project handover · finishing the difficult part
uses.sentence: The report is written and approved; the rest is gravy.
uses.tip: Best among colleagues who already share your tone.

uses.where: Event preparation · chairs are still needed
uses.sentence: We’ve decorated the venue and hired the band, so the rest is gravy.
uses.tip: It sounds relaxed and good-humoured, but may not suit a formal occasion.

uses.where: Informal project update · most work is complete
uses.sentence: The main edits are done; the rest is gravy and should take an hour.
uses.tip: Avoid it in formal reports or messages to senior stakeholders.

origin.summary: This likely developed from British and Australian informal speech, using gravy as the tasty extra that comes after the main meal.

timeline.text: Informal expressions such as “everything else is gravy” appear in British and Australian speech.
The phrase becomes established for the idea that the remaining work is easy or unimportant.
It remains mainly informal and is especially associated with British and Australian English.

cards.opposite: the hard part is still ahead
cards.pitfall: Do not use it when serious risks or substantial work remain; “the rest is gravy” can make unfinished work sound trivial.

cards.term: the shoe is on the other foot
cards.register: Common at work and in conversation
cards.meaning: The situation has changed so that someone now has the disadvantage, advantage or role that previously belonged to someone else.
cards.nuance: It emphasizes a reversal in power, luck or circumstances. It often sounds conversational and may be slightly dramatic, so it suits informal discussion more than very formal writing.
cards.literal: A shoe that was on one foot has moved to the other, creating a simple picture of things being reversed.

uses.sentence: We moved the deadline to Friday, so now the shoe is on the other foot and the client is waiting on us.
uses.highlight: the shoe is on the other foot
uses.tip: Use it when both sides have genuinely exchanged positions or pressures.

uses.sentence: I finally admitted I’m better at planning than cooking, so the shoe is on the other foot this week.
uses.highlight: the shoe is on the other foot
uses.tip: It adds humor when roles change between two people.

uses.sentence: After years of waiting for approval, our legal team is now waiting on us, and the shoe is on the other foot.
uses.highlight: the shoe is on the other foot
uses.tip: It works in an informal update, but name the changed roles for clarity.

origin.summary: The exact source is uncertain, but the expression grew from older language about changing feet, legs or positions in contests and everyday life.

timeline.text: Similar expressions about the boot, shoe or leg being on the other side appear in descriptions of reversed positions and fortunes.
The wording becomes established in English conversation for a reversal of circumstances.
It remains a common idiom for describing changed advantages, roles or power.

similar: the boot is on the other foot
cards.opposite: the shoe is on the same foot
cards.pitfall: Use the phrase only when there is a clear reversal; for a minor change, simply describing the new situation is clearer.

cards.register: Common at work and in everyday life
cards.meaning: A situation or event must continue even when there are problems, delays or setbacks.
cards.nuance: It can sound determined and practical, but sometimes suggests that people are expected to ignore serious problems. Make sure it fits the situation rather than dismissing a genuine concern.
cards.literal: A theatre performance continues even if something goes wrong backstage.

uses.where: Team stand-up · a release is delayed
uses.sentence: The show must go on, so we’ll release the core features today and add the remaining updates next week.
uses.tip: Use it to focus on a workable plan, not to brush aside risks or blockers.

uses.sentence: The show must go on, so we’ll put on some music and keep the evening going.
uses.tip: It works well when a minor problem should not derail the occasion.

uses.sentence: Some attendees were delayed by the weather, but the show must go on, and the main presentation will begin on time.
uses.tip: Pair it with a concrete update so it sounds reassuring rather than dismissive.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from theatre, where performers continued a production despite accidents, equipment failures or other problems backstage.

timeline.text: The theatrical expression appears in accounts describing a performance continuing despite difficulties.
It expands beyond theatre to describe events and activities carrying on through setbacks.
It is widely used to express resilience or a determination to continue.

cards.pitfall: In a serious situation, this phrase can sound like you value the event more than people’s safety or concerns.

cards.meaning: The situation has changed dramatically, often turning against the person who previously had the advantage.
cards.nuance: This often carries a sense of defeat, justice or revenge, so it can sound triumphant or contemptuous. It fits a major reversal better than an ordinary setback.
cards.literal: A worm reversing its direction, suggesting that the course of events has changed.

uses.sentence: After months of resisting the change, the worm has turned, and senior management has now approved it.
uses.tip: Use it when a long-running situation has reversed, not for a minor inconvenience.

uses.sentence: He won every game last summer, but the worm has turned and she is unbeaten now.
uses.tip: It adds drama and may imply that the earlier advantage was deservedly lost.

uses.sentence: He dismissed every warning, but the worm has turned, and his former strategy is now failing him.
uses.tip: Choose a more neutral phrase such as “the tables have turned” for a less hostile tone.

origin.summary: The image comes from a worm reversing its course. The wording appears in Shakespeare’s Henry IV, Part 2 and later became a broader expression for a reversal of fortune, often involving defeat or revenge.

timeline.text: The expression developed from the image of a worm turning and changing direction.
Shakespeare used the image in Henry IV, Part 2 in connection with a reversal of fortune.
The idiom became established for situations in which someone’s fortunes or control had changed dramatically.
It remains understood as a dramatic, often hostile way to describe a major reversal.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it for a small problem; the phrase implies a striking and often unwelcome reversal.

cards.meaning: To add a final detail or event that completes something, often in a funny, awkward or unwelcome way.
cards.nuance: It often carries a slightly ironic tone, suggesting that the last addition pushed an already notable situation over the edge.
cards.literal: To put something on top of something else, like a final layer or topping.

uses.where: Team lunch · describing a hectic morning
uses.sentence: To top it off, the client changed the deadline just before our presentation.
uses.tip: Use it when the final detail adds surprise or mild frustration.

uses.sentence: We lost my keys, got rained on, and then, to top it off, the café closed.
uses.tip: It works well when you are listing mishaps and adding the final mishap.

uses.sentence: The upload failed twice; to top it off, I saved the revised file to the wrong folder.
uses.tip: Keep the tone light unless the extra problem is genuinely serious.

origin.summary: The phrase likely grew from the literal idea of placing a topping on food, then developed the sense of adding a final element to a sequence of events.

timeline.text: The literal phrase referred to putting a final topping on food.
Figurative uses appeared for adding something that completes or punctuates an event.
It commonly introduces an ironic final detail in everyday conversation.

cards.opposite: to end on a high note
cards.pitfall: It often implies that the final detail is unpleasant or absurd, so it may sound insincere when describing something positive.

cards.meaning: A remark used to point out that you had previously warned someone about something that happened.
cards.nuance: It can sound playful when you are close to the other person, but triumphant or smug when you are not. Use it sparingly if you want to make a point without creating tension.
cards.literal: A claim that the listener was previously told about the event that has just happened.

uses.sentence: The report was delayed, and I told you so when we first reviewed the timeline.
uses.tip: Use it lightly when you already have a friendly working relationship.

uses.where: Plans with friends · a familiar warning
uses.sentence: The bus was late, so I told you so when we decided to leave early.
uses.tip: It works best as gentle teasing, especially with friends.

uses.sentence: The client requested the same changes I flagged earlier, so I told you so in my last email.
uses.tip: In professional writing, it may sound smug; consider naming the earlier warning directly.

origin.summary: The phrase probably grew from the older English pattern “I told you so,” used when someone points out that they warned another person before an event.

timeline.text: The basic wording referred to having given someone advance warning.
The expression became a familiar way to claim credit for predicting someone else’s mistake or misfortune.
It remains common in casual speech, often with a teasing or self-important tone.

cards.pitfall: Avoid using it when you need to solve a problem; the remark can distract from the issue and make you sound smug.

cards.meaning: Used to express regret or mild disappointment about an unfortunate situation.
cards.nuance: It is common in everyday conversation, but it can sound insincere if someone is genuinely upset or affected by the situation.
cards.literal: It is unfortunate that this has happened.

uses.sentence: Too bad the deadline moved, but the extra time will help us get it right.
uses.tip: Pair it with something supportive when the problem affects a colleague.

uses.sentence: Too bad you missed the show, but we’ll catch up on everything tomorrow.
uses.tip: Use it lightly when the disappointment is minor.

uses.sentence: Too bad the weather is awful, so let’s postpone our walk until next week.
uses.tip: In writing, add a friendly follow-up to keep the message warm.

origin.summary: The exact origin is uncertain, but the phrase has long been used as a simple expression of regret or disappointment.

timeline.text: The wording developed from expressing that something is bad or unfortunate.
“Too bad” appears in ordinary English writing and conversation.
It remains a common casual expression, though its tone can be dismissive if used carelessly.

cards.pitfall: Do not use “too bad” when the person is truly upset; acknowledge their feelings instead.

cards.meaning: Used mockingly to show that you do not feel sorry about someone’s disappointing experience.
cards.nuance: It is usually teasing or sarcastic rather than genuinely sympathetic. Use it only with people you know well, because it can sound cruel in a serious conversation.
cards.literal: The literal words express sympathy, but the phrase is often meant to sound unserious or dismissive.

uses.where: Chatting after a colleague misses an opportunity
uses.sentence: You booked the wrong meeting? Well, too bad, so sad.
uses.tip: Keep it playful and avoid using it when a colleague is genuinely upset.

uses.where: Teasing a friend about losing a game
uses.sentence: You lost again? Too bad, so sad—I’ll even buy you your next coffee.
uses.tip: A friendly joke or follow-up gesture makes the sarcasm feel less harsh.

uses.sentence: Your flight was delayed for six hours? Too bad, so sad. I’ll send you something to read.
uses.tip: It works best in informal messages; it may sound dismissive in professional email.

origin.summary: Probably grew from an older pattern of mock sympathy, “too bad,” followed by “so sad.” The alliterative version became especially familiar through casual and online speech in the early 21st century.

timeline.text: People used “too bad” as a simple expression of sympathy.
The rhyming addition “so sad” appeared in casual jokes and online exchanges.
It is common as a sarcastic or teasing response, especially among friends.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it to respond to serious hardship, grief or disappointment; it may sound heartless rather than playful.

cards.meaning: After the best time to act has passed, so it is no longer possible or useful to do something.
cards.nuance: It can describe a missed opportunity, a completed deadline or a response that arrives after someone has spoken. It may sound neutral or mildly critical, depending on the context.
cards.literal: Later than the required or useful time.

uses.sentence: We can’t add another feature now; the release date is too close, and it’s too late to test it properly.
uses.tip: Use it to close an unrealistic request and explain why it cannot be changed safely.

uses.sentence: It’s too late to join the dinner, so we’ll order something light and catch up with everyone there.
uses.tip: This use is usually matter-of-fact rather than disappointed.

uses.sentence: I’m sorry, but it’s too late to include this section in tomorrow’s report.
uses.tip: Pair it with a reason or an alternative when you need to soften the refusal.

origin.summary: The word “late” has long meant arriving or acting after the expected time. The intensifier “too” came into common use to show that the delay has passed the point of being acceptable or useful.

timeline.text: The word “late” was used for something happening after its expected time.
The intensifier “too” was added to create the idea of being later than is acceptable or useful.
The phrase is common in everyday speech, workplaces and informal writing.

cards.pitfall: “Too late” can sound blunt; add a brief reason or an alternative when you are declining an offer.
